entry.title: A Day in the Life of Studying Abroad

media:group.media:title: A Day in the Life of Studying Abroad
media:group.media:description:
Join Duke students Helen Jin and Naomi Wordofa as they take you through a day in their lives studying abroad in Tanzania! Activities in their day can include doing field work studying animal footprints, cataloging bones, listening to lectures from anthropology professors, and playing games or watching a movie together.
Through the university course Paleoanthropology Field School: Human Origins Studies at Laetoli in Tanzania, students got the opportunity to camp and study for one month at Laeotoli, a renowned anthropology site located in Tanzania's Ngorongoro Conservation Area.
This video was filmed by Deja Brooks, Duke Class of 2029 student, who also spent one month studying abroad in Tanzania and is a photography and videography intern for Duke University Duke Office of Communications, Marketing and Public Affairs.
To learn more about study abroad opportunities offered at Duke, visit: https://globaled.duke.edu/programs/duke-in-programs/

entry.title: What Can Your Walk Reveal About You? | Why Do You Study That?

media:group.media:title: What Can Your Walk Reveal About You? | Why Do You Study That?
media:group.media:description:
What can something as simple as walking reveal about the human body?
At Duke University's Michael W. Krzyzewski Human Performance Laboratory, better known as the K-Lab, researchers use motion-capture cameras, reflective markers, and force plates to measure what the human eye can't see.
Named for legendary Duke basketball coach Mike Krzyzewski, the K-Lab helps scientists study everything from athletic performance and injury prevention to joint replacements and rehabilitation after spinal cord injuries.
In this episode of Why Do You Study That?, K-Lab director Lou DeFrate and research analyst Tim Lindsay show us how tracking movement can help researchers better understand the human body—and ultimately help people move better.

media:group.media:description:
Nursing student Jake Benoit starts his day in the hospital at 6:30 am. As a second semester Master of Nursing student in the Duke University School of Nursing, Jake spends one day a week in the hospital working with patients. The other days of the week he spends in class, learning through simulations in the Center for Nursing Discovery and studying to become a registered nurse.
In this episode of A Day in the Life at Duke, we follow Jake during his day as he cares for a patient at Duke University Hospital. We also join Jake in the Center for Nursing Discover, a part of the Duke University School of Nursing, for a simulation and skills training with fellow students in his nursing cohort.
The @DukeSchoolOfNursing provides state-of-the-art technology and tools to equip its students to become practice-ready nurses at the earliest stages of their nursing journey. Interested in a career in nursing? To learn more about the Duke University School of Nursing and its program offerings, visit: https://nursing.duke.edu/.

entry.title: Can One Comma Change the Second Amendment?

media:group.media:title: Can One Comma Change the Second Amendment?
media:group.media:description:
Duke law professor Joseph Blocher studies the history, language, and interpretation of the U.S. Constitution—including what punctuation can tell us about how people understand words in historical documents.
In a world where so much of what we read comes to us through computer screens and AI, Blocher argues there’s still value in seeing the real thing.
We visit the Durham Public Library to explore unique copies of the Declaration of Independence. Blocher explains what the significance of looking beyond the words on the screen—and why sometimes, as Blocher puts it, we need to “touch grass.”
These historic documents will be on display at Duke’s Nasher Museum of Art from September 24, 2026, through January 3, 2027.

00:00:02:06 - 00:00:04:05 Entire fields of constitutional law
00:00:04:05 - 00:00:07:21 are built around the meaning of just 1 or 2 words in the document.
00:00:07:23 - 00:00:09:15 Commerce, for example.
00:00:09:15 - 00:00:13:00 I spent a lot of time studying the Second Amendment, which has just 27
00:00:13:00 - 00:00:16:10 words, and people read those words as if they have one comma.
00:00:16:14 - 00:00:19:02 Many historical versions have two commas,
00:00:19:02 - 00:00:22:07 and the version on display at the National Archives has three commas.
00:00:22:13 - 00:00:25:04 And where we put those commas could change the emphasis
00:00:25:04 - 00:00:28:04 and even the meaning of the words themselves.
00:00:28:21 - 00:00:30:13 My name is Joseph Blocker, and I study
00:00:30:13 - 00:00:33:13 constitutional law.
00:00:39:06 - 00:00:41:22 Looking at an original document, I get the same kind of feeling
00:00:41:22 - 00:00:43:14 I get standing in a historic building
00:00:43:14 - 00:00:47:01 or on an old battlefield, which is an invitation to inhabit
00:00:47:01 - 00:00:50:02 the world of the people who, in this case, wrote the document.
00:00:50:03 - 00:00:50:20 Who were they?
00:00:50:20 - 00:00:53:12 Who are they speaking to? What was their goal?
00:00:53:12 - 00:00:56:13 This isn't actually the original declaration.
00:00:56:13 - 00:01:00:07 The Stone Declaration is an 1823 engraving
00:01:00:15 - 00:01:05:03 that was made as a very accurate copy of the original Declaration of Independence.
00:01:05:04 - 00:01:05:10 In fact,
00:01:05:10 - 00:01:09:22 this is the version of the declaration that most Americans recognize today,
00:01:09:23 - 00:01:15:01 and it is one of just 200 copies that were originally commissioned
00:01:15:01 - 00:01:19:13 to preserve the declaration once the original started to deteriorate.
00:01:19:14 - 00:01:22:14 And far fewer than 200 still in circulation.
00:01:23:05 - 00:01:27:12 The error corrections really does make it easier to see these as human
00:01:27:12 - 00:01:31:10 created documents that were imperfect, not just in the ideals
00:01:31:10 - 00:01:34:08 that they articulated, but even just in the way that they're they're written.
00:01:34:08 - 00:01:37:03 There's a missing word which they just added in
00:01:37:03 - 00:01:41:04 with a little carrot, the phrase “all men are created equal”
00:01:41:08 - 00:01:45:05 we understand that much differently and much more capacious than they did
00:01:45:06 - 00:01:46:06 at the time.
00:01:46:06 - 00:01:50:13 So much of what we read is mediated through search engines and AI and screens.
00:01:50:13 - 00:01:53:16 And sometimes it's important to just get back to the originals, to come back
00:01:53:16 - 00:01:57:06 to, to touch grass, as they say, and see where the history actually began.
00:01:57:07 - 00:02:00:10 And the Stone Declaration is about as close as you can get to
00:02:00:11 - 00:02:03:13 being physically present at the founding of the country.
00:02:03:13 - 00:02:07:19 Well, this is so much more rich than seventh grade civics was, right.
00:02:07:21 - 00:02:10:16 Seeing this first hand is a whole other dimension of the experience.
00:02:10:16 - 00:02:12:13 As a Durham native who spent a lot of my childhood
00:02:12:13 - 00:02:15:02 at the Durham Public Library, it is especially exciting.
00:02:15:02 - 00:02:15:23 It makes me so happy
00:02:15:23 - 00:02:19:15 and proud that the people of my hometown get to engage with this document today.
00:02:19:17 - 00:02:23:02 I hope that all students of constitutional law and American history
00:02:23:03 - 00:02:26:02 see themselves as authors of an ongoing story
00:02:26:02 - 00:02:28:23 where all of us have something to say and something to contribute.
